                    ### Question
                    A 25-year-old woman presented to an urgent care center with a complaint of a cough for more than 3 weeks that was accompanied by night sweats, weight loss, and malaise. On physical examination, the patient had slightly pale palpebral conjunctivae bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, but with no adventitious breath sounds in the lung fields bilaterally. The remainder of the physical examination was routine. The patient was started on a drug regimen that was to be taken for 6 months. On follow-up after 2 months, the ALT and AST levels were elevated. Which of the following anti-tubercular drug could have contributed to this labor result?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Rifampicin
opb. Pyrazinamide
opc. Isoniazid
opd. Streptomycin
ope. Ethambutol

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with symptoms consistent with tuberculosis (cough, night sweats, weight loss, malaise) and has cervical lymphadenopathy. She was started on a 6-month anti-tubercular regimen, which typically includes drugs such as isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and streptomycin. Follow-up revealed elevated ALT and AST levels, indicating potential hepatotoxicity. Pyrazinamide is well-documented to cause hepatotoxicity and is a likely contributor to the elevated liver enzymes. Isoniazid can also cause liver enzyme elevation but is less commonly associated with significant hepatotoxicity compared to pyrazinamide. Rifampicin, streptomycin, and ethambutol are generally not associated with significant liver enzyme elevation. Therefore, the most likely drug contributing to the elevated liver enzymes is pyrazinamide.
